title: What is the difference between batch processing and stream processing — batch processes large chunks of data at once (e.g., every night), stream processes data as soon as it arrives (e.g., real-time)?
shortTitle: Difference between batch processing and stream processing

s1_definition.profdef: Batch processing collects data over a window of time into a bounded dataset and processes the whole chunk in one scheduled run, optimizing for throughput and cost. Stream processing handles an unbounded sequence of events continuously, processing each event or a tiny micro-batch as it arrives, optimizing for low latency. The core difference is bounded-and-delayed versus unbounded-and-immediate.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India in two modes. Batch is like the bank's end-of-day reconciliation: the staff wait until midnight, take the whole day's pile of transactions, and process them together in one big run — cheaper and simpler, but you only learn today's totals tomorrow morning. Stream is like the fraud desk watching each card swipe live: the moment Rajesh's card is swiped in two cities within one minute, an alert fires immediately. Batch answers "what happened yesterday"; streaming answers "what is happening right now".
s1_definition.oneliner: Batch processes a finished pile of data on a schedule; streaming processes each event the instant it arrives.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Batch processing collects data over a window of time into a bounded dataset and processes the whole chunk in one scheduled run, optimizing for throughput and cost. Stream processing handles an unbounded sequence of events continuously, processing each event or a tiny micro-batch as it arrives, optimizing for low latency. The core difference is bounded-and-delayed versus unbounded-and-immediate.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India in two modes. Batch is like the bank's end-of-day reconciliation: the staff wait until midnight, take the whole day's pile of transactions, and process them together in one big run — cheaper and simpler, but you only learn today's totals tomorrow morning. Stream is like the fraud desk watching each card swipe live: the moment Rajesh's card is swiped in two cities within one minute, an alert fires immediately. Batch answers "what happened yesterday"; streaming answers "what is happening right now".

**One line to remember:** Batch processes a finished pile of data on a schedule; streaming processes each event the instant it arrives.

sections.s2_technical:
Batch processing works on a bounded dataset — a dataset with a known start and end, like "all transactions for 2024-10-29". A scheduler kicks off a job, the job reads the entire chunk, performs transformations and aggregations, writes the result, and stops until the next scheduled run. Because the job sees all the data at once, it can do heavy operations like large joins and full re-sorts efficiently, and it is easy to re-run if it fails. The cost is latency: results are only as fresh as the schedule. In Java you might express a batch aggregation as `txns.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Transaction::getAccountId, Collectors.reducing(BigDecimal.ZERO, Transaction::getAmount, BigDecimal::add)))` which sums every account's spend in one pass over the whole day's list.

Stream processing works on an unbounded dataset — events keep arriving forever with no natural end. A long-running job consumes events continuously and emits results continuously. Because you never see "all the data", computations over time must use windows (for example, a one-minute tumbling window of card swipes). You poll a stream like `records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(200))` and handle each `ConsumerRecord` immediately, updating running state. Streaming shines for use cases where freshness is the whole point: fraud detection, live dashboards, and real-time limits.

A senior nuance is that "stream" is often really micro-batch. Spark Structured Streaming groups events into tiny batches every few hundred milliseconds — simpler and higher throughput but with a small latency floor. True record-at-a-time engines like Flink process each event individually for the lowest latency. Another nuance is correctness over time: streaming must deal with event-time versus processing-time, late data, and watermarks, which batch mostly sidesteps because it processes a complete, settled chunk. Finally, the two are not enemies — the lambda and kappa architectures combine a fast streaming layer for immediacy with a batch layer for completeness and correction.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India needs an end-of-day report of total spend per account. There is no rush; it just needs to be complete and correct by morning. This is exactly batch processing — we wait for the full day's transactions and process them in one run.

Problem 2 — The fraud team needs to catch suspicious activity the instant it happens, not tomorrow. This is exactly stream processing — each transaction is evaluated the moment it arrives, and an alert fires immediately if an amount crosses a threshold.

Problem 3 — The bank wants to see the clear contrast on the same data: the same transactions, once as a nightly batch total and once as a live stream of alerts. This shows why both modes coexist.

The mini-project defines `Transaction` as the event. `BatchProcessor` has `runEndOfDay()` which takes the whole list and produces per-account totals. `StreamProcessor` has `onEvent()` which is called once per transaction as it "arrives" and immediately raises an alert for any transaction above a limit. The demo feeds the same five transactions through both to show batch-completeness versus stream-immediacy.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is five transactions over five minutes for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001), two of which exceed the 100000 alert threshold.

Step 1 — Stream mode starts. T1 (1200) arrives and is processed immediately; it is below the threshold so it logs OK. The result is known the instant the event is seen.

Step 2 — T2 (150000) arrives one minute later and is processed immediately; it exceeds the threshold so a fraud alert fires at once. Streaming did not wait for the day to end.

Step 3 — T3, T4, T5 each arrive and are each handled on arrival; T4 (250000) triggers a second immediate alert. By the end of the stream, two alerts have already fired in real time.

Step 4 — Batch mode starts on the same five transactions, now treated as a complete bounded pile. It walks every record and sums per account: Rajesh gets 1200 + 150000 + 800 = 152000, Priya gets 5000 + 250000 = 255000.

Step 5 — Output. Streaming produced immediate per-event alerts; batch produced complete per-account totals in one run. Same data, two very different value propositions.

```
INFO: --- STREAM MODE (immediate, per event) ---
INFO: OK: SAV2001 spent 1200.00
SEVERE: FRAUD ALERT: SAV2001 spent 150000.00 (> 100000.00) at 2024-10-29T10:01
INFO: OK: CUR3001 spent 5000.00
SEVERE: FRAUD ALERT: CUR3001 spent 250000.00 (> 100000.00) at 2024-10-29T10:03
INFO: OK: SAV2001 spent 800.00
INFO: --- BATCH MODE (end of day, whole pile) ---
INFO: BATCH end-of-day run over 5 transactions
INFO: ACCOUNT SAV2001 total=152000.00
INFO: ACCOUNT CUR3001 total=255000.00
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Batch processing and stream processing are two ways of handling data that differ mainly in whether the dataset is bounded and whether results can be delayed. Batch processing collects data over a window into a bounded dataset with a known start and end, then processes the whole chunk in one scheduled run. Because the job sees everything at once, it can do heavy joins and aggregations efficiently and is trivial to re-run, but results are only as fresh as the schedule. Stream processing handles an unbounded sequence of events continuously, processing each event the moment it arrives, which gives very low latency at the cost of more complexity.

The deeper technical difference is how you compute over time. In batch you simply process a complete, settled chunk, so you rarely worry about ordering. In streaming you never see all the data, so computations over time rely on windows like a one-minute tumbling window, and you must handle event-time versus processing-time, late data, and watermarks. A senior nuance I always mention is that much of what people call streaming is actually micro-batch, like Spark Structured Streaming grouping events every few hundred milliseconds, whereas true record-at-a-time engines like Flink process each event individually for the lowest latency.

The two modes are not rivals; they complement each other, which is the whole idea behind lambda and kappa architectures that run a fast speed layer alongside a complete batch layer.

In my project at the National Bank of India I used both on the same transaction data. The fraud team needed immediacy, so a streaming job evaluated each transaction the instant it arrived and fired an alert the moment Rajesh's or Priya's spend crossed a threshold. The finance team needed completeness, so a nightly batch job took the whole day's transactions and produced correct per-account totals in a single run. Streaming answered what is happening right now, and batch answered what happened over the whole day, and the bank genuinely needed both.

---

keyPoints: Batch: process accumulated data periodically (hourly, daily)
Stream: process data continuously in real-time
Kappa architecture: stream-only — simplify by treating everything as stream
